data.name: Resistance exercise / mechanical load
data.description: Mechanical loading of skeletal muscle, the physiological stimulus for hypertrophy, acting through mTORC1.

reading_levels.student: Mechanical loading of skeletal muscle, the physiological stimulus for hypertrophy, acting through mTORC1.
reading_levels.research: One of the very few places in this map where the causal chain has been interrupted in living humans: rapamycin blocks the early contraction-induced rise in muscle protein synthesis (DRU2009). It also blunted ERK1/2 in the same volunteers, so the block shows that the response is rapamycin-sensitive, not that mTORC1 alone carries it. The upstream route is only partly IGF-1-dependent – mechanical load reaches mTORC1 through mechanisms that do not require circulating growth factor, which is why loading and hormone signalling are not interchangeable.

studies.title: Akt/mTOR pathway is a crucial regulator of skeletal muscle hypertrophy and can prevent muscle atrophy in vivo
studies.authors: Bodine SC; Stitt TN; Gonzalez M; Kline WO; Stover GL; Bauerlein R; Zlotchenko E; Scrimgeour A; Lawrence JC; Glass DJ; Yancopoulos GD

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: Akt/mTOR signalling is necessary and sufficient to drive skeletal-muscle hypertrophy and counteract atrophy in vivo.

studies.title: Rapamycin administration in humans blocks the contraction-induced increase in skeletal muscle protein synthesis
studies.authors: Drummond MJ; Fry CS; Glynn EL; Dreyer HC; Dhanani S; Timmerman KL; Volpi E; Rasmussen BB

evidence.label: Human study
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

studies.finding: Rapamycin given before resistance exercise blocked the early (1–2 h) post-exercise rise in human muscle protein synthesis, which was about 40% in the control group. Rapamycin also blocked the rise in ERK1/2 phosphorylation and blunted MNK1, so the authors conclude that mTORC1 drives the response only in part. The study measured acute protein synthesis, not muscle growth.

relations.claim: Resistance exercise / mechanical load activates mTORC1
relations.mechanism: Mechanical loading raises mTORC1 signalling in skeletal muscle. Rapamycin given to human volunteers blocks the contraction-induced increase in muscle protein synthesis, placing mTORC1 causally between the load and the response.
relations.mechanism_beginner: Working a muscle raises mTORC1 activity in it. When volunteers took rapamycin, the rise in muscle protein building after exercise was blocked, so in people, and not only in cell dishes, mTORC1 sits between the effort and the response. The map draws one arrow, but load reaches mTORC1 by several routes, and this result does not show which one carries the signal.
relations.boundary: Compressed: load reaches mTORC1 through several routes, only some of which need IGF-1, and the map draws one arrow. The human evidence establishes that mTORC1 is required, not which upstream route carries the signal.
